events.title: Democratic opening: electoral democracy index rose 0.48 over 5 years
events.detail: From 0.18 in 1948 to 0.66 in 1953. Derived by detecting a sustained shift of at least 0.2 index points over 5 years; marked at the steepest year of the episode.
events.contested: V-Dem indices are aggregated expert judgements with published uncertainty intervals. A shift of this size is well outside the noise, but the exact year is a property of the detection rule, not a documented event.

events.title: Emergency declared
events.detail: A state of internal emergency was proclaimed, suspending elections, detaining opposition figures and imposing press censorship. It lasted until March 1977.
events.contested: Read by some as an aberration that democratic institutions survived, and by others as evidence of how few structural checks existed on executive power. Economic readings differ too - the period saw both forced sterilisation campaigns and a temporary fall in industrial unrest.
events.refs: ["Proclamation of Emergency under Article 352, 25 June 1975", "Shah Commission of Inquiry, Interim and Final Reports (1978)"]

events.title: Liberalisation budget ends the licence raj
events.detail: Facing reserves covering roughly two weeks of imports, the Narasimha Rao government devalued the rupee, abolished industrial licensing for most sectors, cut peak import tariffs and opened many industries to foreign equity.
events.contested: Growth accelerated after 1991, but the size of the reform's own contribution is argued over. One school dates the trend break to the 1980s, when a milder pro-business shift was already under way, and treats 1991 as consolidation of a trend rather than its start. Others argue the 1980s expansion was debt-financed and unsustainable, and that 1991 is what made growth durable.
events.refs: ["Government of India, Union Budget speech, 24 July 1991", "Rodrik & Subramanian, 'From Hindu Growth to Productivity Surge' (IMF Staff Papers, 2005)", "Panagariya, 'India: The Emerging Giant' (2008)"]

events.title: Demonetisation of high-value currency notes
events.detail: 500- and 1000-rupee notes, roughly 86% of currency in circulation by value, were withdrawn as legal tender with four hours' notice.
events.contested: Stated aims were to destroy black money, counterfeit currency and terror financing. The RBI later reported that almost all withdrawn notes returned to the banking system. Supporters point to accelerated digital payment adoption and a widened tax base; critics point to the contraction in informal-sector activity. The measured GDP effect is disputed partly because the informal economy is poorly captured by national accounts in the first place.
events.refs: ["RBI Annual Report 2017-18, chapter on currency management", "Government of India Economic Survey 2016-17, chapter 3"]
